title: This too is for good (Taanit 21a)
hookLine: Nachum of Gamzu met every setback by saying this too is for good

lines: THE TRAIN, THE COFFEE, THE NO.
cards: You miss the train. The coffee spills. The email you were waiting for says no.
There's a split second before you react when you get to decide what this is. A disaster? An annoyance?
A story you'll tell later? One sage in the Talmud filled that split second with the same three Hebrew words, every single time. Gam zu l'tovah.
This too is for good. People called him Nachum Ish Gam Zu: Nachum, the this-too man.

teach.h: A CHEST OF JEWELS FOR ROME.
teach.b: Tractate Taanit tells it. The Jewish community wanted to send a gift to the emperor in Rome, and chose Nachum to carry it, because miracles seemed to follow him. They gave him a chest full of jewels.

On the way he stopped at an inn, and in the night the innkeepers opened the chest, stole the jewels, and filled it with dirt. In the morning Nachum saw what had happened, and said: this too is for good.
At the palace he opened the chest before the emperor.
Dirt. The emperor was furious and ordered him killed. Then the story turns.
A stranger appeared among the emperor's advisers; the Talmud says it was the prophet Elijah. Maybe, he said, this is the dirt of their ancestor Abraham, who threw dust that turned into swords.
The Romans tried it against a province they had never managed to conquer, and it worked. Nachum went home honored, his chest full of treasure. One careful point.
The same passage says Nachum lived with great suffering: he was blind, with no hands or feet, and his body was covered in sores. So his three words weren't a smile pasted over pain.
They were a way of trusting that the story isn't finished yet.
Nachum doesn't say this is good.
He says this, too, is for good. The word for does a lot of work.

how: Gam zu l'tovah is an everyday Jewish expression, said when plans fall through; a related saying in the Talmud, attributed to Rabbi Akiva, is that everything the Merciful One does is for good.

o: the sage who said this too is for good
a Levite who guarded the Temple gates at night
the Roman emperor who was sent a gift chest

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Nachum said gam zu l'tovah only when things went well
he said it at every setback, even the dirt in the chest.
the phrase means this is good
it means this too is for good: the story isn't finished.
the Talmud says Nachum lived with great suffering
blind and badly afflicted, and still he said the words.

games.q: you open the emperor's gift chest and find dirt instead of jewels. what do you say?
games.why: Nachum said gam zu l'tovah, and in the story the dirt turned into the emperor's victory.

practice: Pick one small annoyance from this week, not a tragedy, just the delayed package or the canceled plan, and notice the story you told yourself about it. Then try Nachum's words: gam zu l'tovah, this too is for good.
You don't have to know how; leave the ending open, and notice if anything loosens.

wordCard.voice: Nachum, called the this-too man, who met every setback with three Hebrew words: gam zu l'tovah, this too is for good, trusting the story wasn't over.

orig.note: Hebrew: this too is for good.

carryVoice: Your line: this too for the good. The ending isn't written yet. See you tomorrow.
